claims.text: The initial alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution with a near-homogeneous elemental distribution.
Mg clustering is the initial step in the alloy's microstructural evolution during annealing.
Mg clusters act as nucleation sites for Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
The nucleated Mg-rich intermetallic compounds subsequently grow by diffusion.
The Mg-rich intermetallic compounds may be Laves or B2-type phases.
Finely dispersed Mg-rich intermetallics impede the transport of oxygen and corrosive species.
Impeded transport of oxygen and corrosive species supports surface passivation.
A fine dispersion of intermetallics preserves corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Continued annealing causes the intermetallic compounds to grow and coalesce.
Longer annealing times or higher temperatures promote coarse, localized continuous intermetallic networks.
Coarsened intermetallic networks alter grain-boundary chemistry and diffusion paths.
Continuous intermetallic networks along grain boundaries compromise protective oxide and corrosion layers.
Moderate annealing durations retain corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
Intermetallic coarsening increases corrosion rates relative to the initial state.
Intermetallic coarsening compromises high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
The morphology-dependent transition is relevant over approximately 500–700°C and exposures from several hours to a few hundred hours.
The exact kinetics and thermodynamics of Mg clustering and intermetallic transformation are unresolved.
Variations in alloy composition or processing may alter phase stability and intermetallic growth kinetics.
